question: What must follow if these assumptions are true?

servedio2014.cite: Servedio et al. (2014). Not just a theory—the utility of mathematical models in evolutionary biology. PLoS Biology 12(12): e1002017.
servedio2014.checked: every quote read word for word in the open-access full text from Europe PMC (PMC4260780, full-text XML) on 20 Nov 2026; places are the article's sections and boxes; reference numbers are left out of the quotes

steps.title: Start from a claim
steps.text: Begin with an explanation stated in words: this happens because of that.

quotes.text: Progress in science often begins with verbal hypotheses meant to explain why certain biological phenomena exist.

steps.title: Write the assumptions
steps.text: Turn each ingredient of the claim into a precise mathematical assumption, and say which ones carry the hypothesis.

quotes.text: Proof-of-concept models, used in many fields, test the validity of verbal chains of logic by laying out the specific assumptions mathematically.
quotes.where: section “Proof-of-Concept Models: Testing Verbal Logic in Evolutionary Biology”

steps.title: Derive
steps.text: Work out with proofs or closed-form solutions what the assumptions imply. Mathematics, not intuition, does this step.

quotes.text: The results that follow from these assumptions emerge through the principles of mathematics, which reduces the possibility of logical errors at this step of the process.
quotes.where: section “Proof-of-Concept Models: Testing Verbal Logic in Evolutionary Biology”

steps.title: Compare with the claim
steps.text: Set the derived result beside what the words predicted. Where they differ, the verbal argument had a gap.

quotes.text: to test the validity of a verbal model, precise predictions from a mathematical analysis of the assumptions are compared against verbal predictions.
quotes.where: section “Proof-of-Concept Models: Testing Verbal Logic in Evolutionary Biology”

steps.title: Check against nature
steps.text: The derivation is right by construction; whether it applies is an empirical question about the assumptions.

quotes.text: These tests are not “tests of the model”; the model is correct in that its predictions follow mathematically from its assumptions.
empirical support is essential to ensure that key assumptions of mathematical models are biologically realistic.

model-assumptions.text: if they do not match the intent of the verbal hypothesis, then the mathematical model is not a true test of the verbal one.

limits: The card's defining reference, May (2004) in Science, has not been read for this page; the steps follow Servedio et al. (2014), written for evolutionary biology but, in their words, about models used in many fields.
The card's examples (Carnot's limit, Nash equilibrium) are not worked through here.
